title: Should you use an AI agent builder or buy a support-native platform?
summary: Weighing an AI agent builder against a support-native platform? See when it makes sense to keep building, and when it’s smarter to buy instead.
body_markdown:
Say someone on your support team builds an AI agent that drafts answers from your help docs. You try it on a few straightforward questions, and the replies are pretty good. After a little editing, they’re ready to send.


You can imagine why the team would want to use it more. But what happens when a customer asks about an issue your dev team is still investigating? Before it answers, the agent needs to know what your team has already told that account (and whether it should even answer to begin with).


You could keep adding to your AI agent builder setup, but you need to be realistic about whether your team has the time and resources to maintain it. This guide weighs that work against buying a support-native platform to explore when each approach makes the most sense.


## The core components of an AI agent builder


Ask AI view from Pylon


An AI agent builder is a platform or framework your team uses to create and configure AI agents. The builder is where you define how an agent works; the agent itself carries out tasks, like investigating a support question or drafting a reply.


A no-code AI agent builder platform lets you create agents through visual tools or natural-language instructions. Visual builders often allow for dragging nodes onto a canvas, with each node representing a step like a model call or tool action.


Building AI agents with code-first frameworks gives your dev team more control, but DIY agents also require more technical work to build and maintain.


Either way,[setting up AI agents](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-set-up-ai-agents) means connecting a few core components:


- **Reasoning engine.** A language model interprets the request and decides what to do next based on the instructions and information available.
- **Memory systems.** Memory retains information across steps or conversations so the agent can refer back to earlier details, like which troubleshooting steps a customer has already tried. Your team defines what gets saved and when the agent can access it.
- **Planning and orchestration.** Orchestration coordinates workflow execution, including which tools to call and when to pause for human input.
- **Tool connections.** APIs or MCP connectors let an AI agent retrieve information and take actions in other systems. Your team controls which tools the agent can use and what those tools allow it to do.


## Why general-purpose AI agent builders feel like enough (at first)


If your team already uses OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, those are natural places to try out a support task. You can give the AI your help docs and instructions, then check whether the output saves you time.


An AI agent can pull details from a ticket thread and draft a summary of the problem for your dev team handoff notes, including what the customer has already tried. For this kind of task, the teammate handling the ticket reviews the summary before passing it along.


If you’re just getting started, that’s often a manageable way to begin[using AI agents](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-use-ai-agents) . The task has clear boundaries, and someone who knows the issue checks the result. If the agent misses a detail, that person can fill it in.


With one owner and a narrow scope, there’s relatively little coordination to worry about.


## The gaps in a DIY AI agent for customer support


Once more people depend on the AI agent, it’s no longer reasonable for the original builder to check every result or fill in every missing detail. An AI agent for customer support needs to work even when its creator is unavailable.


A lightweight DIY setup may leave your team with gaps like these:


- **No persistent account context.** Someone has to supply account details and ticket history before the agent can give an appropriate answer.
- **No built-in escalation logic.** Your team has to define when the agent should stop and who takes over.
- **No audit trail.** Without records of responses and their sources, your team can’t easily investigate a disputed answer.
- **No native connection.** Your team has to manually supply and update information from your ticketing system or knowledge base.
- **No governance over changes.** Anyone with edit access could change the agent’s instructions without others’ approval, affecting how it responds to customers.
- **No reuse across channels.** Siloed **** email, Slack, and[customer portal](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/build-a-customer-portal) **** workflows — without integration across platforms — force teams to make updates in multiple places.


General-purpose builders can address many of those gaps, but someone needs to configure and maintain the solution. And the gaps become even harder to ignore when a handoff loses context or nobody can explain why the agent gave a particular answer.[Pylon’s Skills](https://www.usepylon.com/ai-agents/skills) workflows are reusable, no-code instructions that define what an agent should check, which actions it can take, and when it needs human approval.


## 5 of the best platforms for AI agent building


Agent runbook view from Pylon


If you’re still at the stage where an AI agent builder can handle your team’s needs, here’s how five platforms approach that work:


- [Dify](https://dify.ai/workflows) **(low-code/visual).** Connect model calls, knowledge sources, and tools on a visual canvas to build multi-step workflows. Dify also offers a self-hosted option in which your team runs the deployment.
- [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/) **(no-code).** A **** no-code AI agent builder that lets your team create workflows visually, with code available for custom functions.
- [Microsoft Copilot Studio](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/microsoft-copilot-studio) **(low-code).** Build agents through a graphical interface, with connections to Microsoft services and other systems.
- [CrewAI](https://crewai.com/) **(code-first).** Define agents with distinct roles and coordinate their tasks through crews and structured flows.
- [LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview) **(code-first).** Build custom agents from models and tools, with LangGraph available for more complex orchestration.


Each tool gives your team a way to build agent behavior. But before you deploy an agent for customer-facing use cases, be sure to decide who owns testing and upkeep. You’ll still need to connect that behavior to your support processes. And before you commit, check which features require paid plans and how usage costs could grow as you add use cases for workflow automation and other tasks.

## FAQ


### What’s the best no-code AI agent builder?


The best choice of no-code AI agent builders depends on what you want to automate and which systems the agent needs to access. MindStudio and Dify offer visual tools for building agents. For customer support, also check how much work it takes to connect account context and configure human handoffs.


### Can I use ChatGPT to build an AI agent?


Technically, yes, ChatGPT can help with building AI agents by drafting instructions, developing code, and testing responses. But an agent that runs in your own product needs a separate implementation, like an application built with OpenAI’s APIs, that offers access controls and a reliable way to escalate issues to your team.


### What can I automate with AI agents?


Common use cases include ticket summaries, request categorization, troubleshooting information collection, and answers based on approved documentation. Begin[support automation](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/support-automation-tools) with a task your team can easily check, then expand once you understand where the agent needs help.


### How does an AI agent builder work?


You define the agent’s instructions, connect its knowledge sources, and give it access to tools. In a visual builder, nodes represent individual steps and connections define how execution moves between them. The builder lets you test the results before you deploy the agent. During a task, the agent uses the available information and tools to decide its next step.
